title: Genesis 40:1–23

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Classic comment on dreams in prison, and interpretations that belong to God, from both sides of the debate.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: We should not have had this story of Pharaoh's butler and baker recorded in scripture, if it had not been serviceable to Joseph's preferment. The world stands for the sake of the church, and is governed for its good. Observe, [1.] Two of the great officers of Pharaoh's court having offended the king are committed to prison.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Gen 40:1)

reformed.quote: We have already seen, that when Joseph was in bonds, God cared for him. For whence arose the relaxation afforded him, but from the divine favor? Therefore, God, before he opened the door for his servant's deliverance, entered into the very prison to sustain him with his strength.

context: In prison Joseph is assigned to Pharaoh’s cupbearer and baker. Each dreams; Joseph says interpretations belong to God. The cupbearer will be restored in three days, the baker hanged. Joseph asks to be remembered. On Pharaoh’s birthday both words come true—and the cupbearer forgets him.

verses.text: After these things, the butler of the king of Egypt and his baker offended their lord, the king of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: Two officers fall by their own offense. Guilt is personal: they sinned against their lord. Prison will become a place of meeting, not because they were puppets, but because wrongs have grave consequences.
verses.reformedNotes: Offense, then the king’s house. God is already steering Joseph’s path by other men’s failures. Providence uses even palace scandal without making God the author of their sin.

verses.text: Pharaoh was angry with his two officers, the chief cup bearer and the chief baker.
verses.arminianNotes: Pharaoh’s anger is a human king’s choice. Rank does not cancel accountability: chief cupbearer and chief baker still answer to their lord—and to God who sees courts as well as pits.
verses.reformedNotes: Royal wrath is grave, and it is not outside the Lord’s hand. The same God who humbled Joseph by false charge now brings two chiefs down beside him for a purpose Joseph cannot yet see.

verses.text: He put them in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, into the prison, the place where Joseph was bound.
verses.arminianNotes: The two officials are held in the same prison and the same house as Joseph. Their custody meets Joseph’s confinement. Location is not fate that erases agency; it is the setting where they will soon be asked to trust God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: The captain’s house is no accident. God parks the two dreams beside the interpreter He has already placed there. Confinement is the appointed waiting room of chapter 41.

verses.text: The captain of the guard assigned them to Joseph, and he took care of them. They stayed in prison many days.
verses.arminianNotes: Joseph attends them—faithful service in a cell. Grace enables care for fellow prisoners without guaranteeing a quick exit. The some time is a wait they must inhabit.
verses.reformedNotes: Appointment from the captain, attendance from Joseph: means under providence. God trains His servant in hidden faithfulness while the clock of some time runs toward the dreams.

verses.text: They both dreamed a dream, each man his dream, in one night, each man according to the interpretation of his dream, the cup bearer and the baker of the king of Egypt, who were bound in the prison.
verses.arminianNotes: The two dreams carry two different meanings. God can speak in the night; the hearers remain responsible for what they do with the word. Distinct dreams refuse a one-size omen.
verses.reformedNotes: Night visions in a cell are the Lord’s sending, not random sleep. Each dream carries its own interpretation because God authors both the riddle and the reading.

verses.text: Joseph came in to them in the morning, and saw them, and saw that they were sad.
verses.arminianNotes: He notices downcast faces. Compassion is a chosen attention: Joseph could have ignored fellow inmates. Grace trains the eyes to see trouble before it speaks.
verses.reformedNotes: Morning mercy: the interpreter arrives already seeing. God who gave the dreams also gives Joseph sight for their trouble, so the word will not sit unasked.

verses.text: He asked Pharaoh’s officers who were with him in custody in his master’s house, saying, “Why do you look so sad today?”
verses.arminianNotes: A simple question opens the door. Ministry often starts with honest inquiry. They are still officers, still in custody, still free to answer or stay shut.
verses.reformedNotes: The question is pastoral and providential. Joseph’s “why” is the means by which God draws the dreams into the open for interpretation.

verses.text: They said to him, “We have dreamed a dream, and there is no one who can interpret it.” Joseph said to them, “Don’t interpretations belong to God? Please tell it to me.”
verses.arminianNotes: No court magician is at hand. Joseph points away from himself: interpretations belong to God—then invites them to tell. The gift is no illusion; so is their choice to speak. God sincerely gives light; they must still open the dream.
verses.reformedNotes: Joseph refuses a technician’s pride. Meaning is God’s property. “Please tell it to me” is the appointed means by which the Lord will interpret—not Joseph’s genius, but God’s word through His servant.
verses.keyContrast: Both deny that dreams are decoded by human craft. Arminians emphasize a sincere offer of God’s light that the officers may receive or withhold; Calvinists stress that interpretation is God’s sovereign gift, effectually given through Joseph.

verses.text: The chief cup bearer told his dream to Joseph, and said to him, “In my dream, behold, a vine was in front of me,
verses.arminianNotes: He tells the dream. Trusting Joseph with the night-vision is a responsible step toward the God Joseph named. Revelation meets a willing speaker.
verses.reformedNotes: The cupbearer speaks because God is already moving the story. The vine will mean life restored—first heard in a prison, not a palace.

verses.text: and in the vine were three branches. It was as though it budded, it blossomed, and its clusters produced ripe grapes.
verses.arminianNotes: Three branches, sudden fruit: the dream is vivid and particular. God can use created images without turning nature into a fate-chart. The man must still hear the reading.
verses.reformedNotes: Bud, blossom, grape in haste: the Lord packs three days into a vine. Details are His, not leftover decoration.

verses.text: Pharaoh’s cup was in my hand; and I took the grapes, and pressed them into Pharaoh’s cup, and I gave the cup into Pharaoh’s hand.”
verses.arminianNotes: He dreams his old work: cup in hand, juice for Pharaoh. Hope of restoration is pictured before it is promised. The dream invites faith in the God who interprets, not in the cup itself.
verses.reformedNotes: Office restored is shown before it happens. God previews what He will do on the third day. The cupbearer’s craft is the canvas; the Painter is the Lord.

verses.text: Joseph said to him, “This is its interpretation: the three branches are three days.
verses.arminianNotes: Joseph speaks as a servant of God’s meaning, not a freelancer. Three days is a clear word: grace gives understanding so the man can receive it. The interpretation is offered as truth to be believed.
verses.reformedNotes: “This is its interpretation”—not a guess. God who owns the meaning now utters it by Joseph. The clock of three days is already set in heaven.

verses.text: Within three more days, Pharaoh will lift up your head, and restore you to your office. You will give Pharaoh’s cup into his hand, the way you did when you were his cup bearer.
verses.arminianNotes: Restoration is promised in time and task: head lifted, office returned, cup placed. Mercy to the cupbearer is particular. He will have to walk back into the job as a man who heard God’s word in prison.
verses.reformedNotes: Pharaoh will lift the head because God has said so. Royal favor is the instrument; the decree is the Lord’s. Restoration as formerly is providence, not luck.

verses.text: But remember me when it is well with you. Please show kindness to me, and make mention of me to Pharaoh, and bring me out of this house.
verses.arminianNotes: Joseph asks to be remembered—kindness, mention, release. The plea is lawful and human: grace does not forbid using means. The cupbearer remains free to keep or drop the request.
verses.reformedNotes: A righteous ask sits beside a sure interpretation. God will use even a forgotten plea (v. 23) on His timetable. Joseph’s desire for the house to open is not unbelief; delay will still serve the promise.

verses.text: For indeed, I was stolen away out of the land of the Hebrews, and here also I have done nothing that they should put me into the dungeon.”
verses.arminianNotes: He names the truth: stolen, then jailed without cause. Innocent suffering is not softened; Joseph does not baptize the pit as his own sin. Asking for justice is compatible with trust in God.
verses.reformedNotes: Joseph was thrown into two pits, and he earned neither. Providence allowed the theft and the false charge without making Joseph guilty. The Lord who records this innocence will also time the exit.

verses.text: When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was good, he said to Joseph, “I also was in my dream, and behold, three baskets of white bread were on my head.
verses.arminianNotes: He speaks because the other word was favorable—hope of a matching mercy. Motive is mixed and still responsible: he wants a good reading. God will not tailor truth to that want.
verses.reformedNotes: Favor in the first dream lures the second telling. God still uses the baker’s desire to surface the baskets. The interpretation will not flatter.

verses.text: In the uppermost basket there were all kinds of baked food for Pharaoh, and the birds ate them out of the basket on my head.”
verses.arminianNotes: Food for Pharaoh, birds eating it: a picture he cannot control. The dream warns before Joseph speaks. Hearers are accountable to face a hard vision, not only a hopeful one.
verses.reformedNotes: Birds at the basket are already the Lord’s sign. What looks like provision is marked for scavenging. God authors the grim detail as surely as the vine’s grapes.

verses.text: Joseph answered, “This is its interpretation. The three baskets are three days.
verses.arminianNotes: Same three-day frame, different end. Joseph does not soften the word to keep a friend. Faithful interpretation serves God, not the hearer’s preference.
verses.reformedNotes: Again, “this is its interpretation.” Same God, same clock, opposite verdict. Truth is not a technique Joseph adjusts; it is given.

verses.text: Within three more days, Pharaoh will lift up your head from off you, and will hang you on a tree; and the birds will eat your flesh from off you.”
verses.arminianNotes: The pun turns cruel: head lifted off. Joseph tells the baker the truth in time to meet God, not to entertain. Hard prophecy is still a sincere word; refusing to hear it would not make it less true.
verses.reformedNotes: Judgment as well as restoration sits in Joseph’s mouth because both sit in God’s counsel. Pharaoh’s rope will fulfill what the Lord has shown. The birds finish the sign.
verses.keyContrast: Both refuse a God who only ever blesses. Arminians typically stress a true warning the baker is responsible to hear; Reformed readers emphasize that the hanging is as appointed as the cupbearer’s restoration.

verses.text: On the third day, which was Pharaoh’s birthday, he made a feast for all his servants, and he lifted up the head of the chief cup bearer and the head of the chief baker among his servants.
verses.arminianNotes: Third day, birthday feast, both heads lifted into public view. Joseph’s word meets the calendar. Court celebration does not undo either man’s accountability before the king—or before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Pharaoh’s feast is the stage God named in the dreams. Birthday and banquet serve the interpretation. The Lord times even a pagan holiday to keep His servant’s word.

verses.text: He restored the chief cup bearer to his position again, and he gave the cup into Pharaoh’s hand;
verses.arminianNotes: Vine-dream kept: office and cup return. Mercy in history confirms the God Joseph confessed. The restored man now owes kindness he is still free to give or withhold.
verses.reformedNotes: Restoration as formerly lands on schedule. God who promised the cup into Pharaoh’s hand now places it there. The word was not a lucky guess.

verses.text: but he hanged the chief baker, as Joseph had interpreted to them.
verses.arminianNotes: The baker dies as interpreted. Two hearers, two ends: the difference was not Joseph playing favorites, but God’s true word meeting two lives. Warning was not bluff.
verses.reformedNotes: “As Joseph had interpreted” is the narrator’s seal. Hanging fulfills the baskets. Providence stands over both outcomes without confusing the judge with the sin that brought the baker down.

verses.text: Yet the chief cup bearer didn’t remember Joseph, but forgot him.
verses.arminianNotes: Forgot: a failure of kindness. Joseph’s plea was sincere; the cupbearer’s memory is responsible and drops. Delay is not proof God failed—it is a man neglecting a brother. Two years will test Joseph’s wait.
verses.reformedNotes: Forgetting is sin and instrument. God will use the blank memory so Joseph rises at Pharaoh’s dream, not a servant’s convenience. The pit lasts until the Lord’s hour, not the cupbearer’s gratitude.
verses.keyContrast: Both take the forgetting as neglect. Arminians stress the cupbearer’s accountable failure to keep a promised kindness; Reformed readers stress that God ordained the delay so Joseph would be remembered on God’s day, not man’s.
